newsitem.title: USA: Dollar mixed after Japanese data, Bundesbank comments.
newsitem.headline: Dollar mixed after Japanese data, Bundesbank comments.

text.p: The dollar rose against the Japanese yen Tuesday on expectations that Japanese interest rates would remain low and as rumours swirled that U.S. officials might tolerate a stronger dollar.
But the dollar fell against the German mark amid speculation that plans for a single European currency, which would make the mark less important, would be delayed.
Machinery orders in Japan, excluding orders for ships and from electric power firms, tumbled in August, a sign of continuing weakness in Japan's economy.

Japan's central bank, the Bank of Japan, has kept interest rates at record lows to bolster economic growth. The drop in machinery orders indicated the central bank would keep rates low even though a senior Japanese politician on Monday predicted a hike in domestic rates after elections are held in less than two weeks.
"I think it means that there is less likelihood of an imminent rate hike," said Mike Malpede, a senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd. "It helps the dollar a little bit against the yen."
Japan's rock bottom rates have hurt the Japanese currency by making yen-denominated deposits less attractive to foreign investors.

The dollar got another boost late in the New York session as rumours swirled that Eisuke Sakakibara, director general of the international finance bureau of Japan's Ministry of Finance, said U.S. officials told him they could tolerate the dollar at an exchange rate of 120 yen.
A source close to the Ministry of Finance in New York said: "We have had no information about that. So, strictly speaking, we can't confirm and we can't deny (it)."
Shortly after the rumour surfaced, the dollar hit 111.70 yen, its high for the day. Nevertheless, some currency traders doubted Sakakibara had made that remark.
"There's definitely yen selling because of this rumour," said Doug Lee, an assistant vice president at Sakura Bank Ltd. "I think it's just a rumour. He would never say something like that."
The dollar fetched 111.69 yen in late New York trading, up from 111.19 yen late Monday. It stood at 1.5296 German marks, down from 1.5312 marks late Monday.

Germany's Bundesbank officials continued to emphasise Tuesday that strict adherence to financial criteria is necessary for European countries to become members of the single currency planned for January 1999.

Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer stressed this point on Monday and his remarks were echoed Tuesday by other officials, including Klaus-Dieter Kuebacher, president of the regional central bank in Berlin.

"They don't want to see window dressing and sort of fictitious accounting from countries who want to participate in the first round of monetary union," said David Gilmore, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
Gilmore said the remarks suggest central bank officials could "argue for and perhaps achieve a delay in monetary union."
Such a delay is typically viewed as beneficial for the mark, which would keep its value as a safe haven currency if monetary union were put off.
The German currency strengthened against some other European currencies and the dollar but profit taking later eroded its gains, traders said.
Elsewhere, the dollar fell to 1.2535 Swiss francs from 1.2545 francs.
The British pound slid to $1.5625 from $1.5639. The dollar rose slightly to Canadian $1.3538 from C$1.3532.
